title: Forest proximity and habitat heterogeneity support insectivorous birds and arthropods in California vineyards
content:
by Eleanor K. MacDonald, Daniel S. Karp, Autumn Turner, Breanna L. Martinico, Houston Wilson, Erin E. Wilson-Rankin, Matthew D. Johnson

Agricultural intensification often simplifies habitat structure, reshaping multi-trophic communities by altering arthropod prey and the insectivorous birds that depend on them throughout the year, particularly during breeding. In vineyards, insectivorous birds may also contribute to pest suppression, creating opportunities to link biodiversity conservation with agroecosystem function. We paired point count bird surveys with concurrent sticky trap arthropod sampling across 20 organic or near-organic vineyards in Napa Valley, California, USA, to test whether the same habitat features predict variation in insectivorous bird guilds and arthropod communities. Specifically, we modeled guild-level bird abundance and arthropod order-level diversity and abundance as a function of habitat heterogeneity at local (50 m) and landscape (1000 m) scales, as well as proximity to forest, riparian, and water habitats. Foliage- and bark-gleaning insectivorous birds were more abundant in locally heterogeneous vineyards close to forest and riparian edges, whereas aerial insectivores were not associated with measured habitat covariates. Several prey-relevant arthropod orders were more abundant closer to forests and in locally heterogeneous sites, while arthropod order-level diversity was not associated with measured habitat covariates. Structural equation modeling demonstrated that forest proximity and landscape-scale heterogeneity indirectly supported foliage-bark gleaners by enhancing large beetle and large fly prey abundances, respectively. Together, our results indicate that increasing habitat heterogeneity within vineyards, coupled with maintaining adjacent natural habitats, can support insectivorous bird assemblages and their prey, with potential benefits for biodiversity and biologically based pest management in vineyard landscapes.
